newsitem.title: INDIA: India economy report gets good marks from industry.
newsitem.headline: India economy report gets good marks from industry.

text.p: India's annual report card on the economy has taken a balanced view of the challenges faced by the economy and spells out the right policy approach needed to accelerate growth, industry leaders said on Tuesday.

The Economic Survey, a report on the state of the economy issued by the Finance Ministry, underlined infrastructure bottlenecks, a slowdown in industrial growth, sluggish exports and rising inflation as areas of concern.

"The emphasis on infrastructure and correction of fiscal imbalance is well placed," said Y.P. Srivastava, deputy secretary general of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).
Srivastava said the survey "takes a very balanced approach" to the challenges faced by the economy.
"The survey looks rosy but spells out that reforms need to be continued," V. Raghuraman, secretary general of Associated Chambers of Commerce (Assocham), told Reuters.
The survey precedes the annual fiscal budget. Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is scheduled to unveil the 1997/98 (April/March) federal budget on February 28.
India began liberalising its economy in 1991, under former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, dismantling decades-old socialist controls.

"The sustained growth of the Indian economy reflected in the Economic Survey 1996/97 is owing to the continuation of the reform process initiated in 1991," the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) said in a statement.

The survey's call for more reforms to lure private investment in the economy reflects recognition within Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's fractious 15-party coalition that India needs to carry forward liberalisation, industry leaders said.
Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition ranges from communists to free-market advocates.
The government has also implicitly acknowledged the need to increase the prices of petroleum products to adjust to rising global crude oil price, Assocham's Raghuraman said.

The survey said the deficit on the oil pool account is expected to balloon to 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) in 1996/97 (April-March) compared with 57 billion ($1.6 billion) in the previous fiscal year.
The oil pool deficit is effectively the amount the government owes state oil companies for selling oil products to Indian consumers below world prices.
Oil companies shoulder the burden of the deficit while they wait for the state to pay them back.
The survey called for a phased deregulation of the existing administered pricing regime to attract more investment into the petroleum industry.
But industry leaders were sceptical India could achieve the survey's forecast of industrial growth of 10 percent in the current fiscal year compared with 11.7 percent a year earlier.
The index of industrial production grew by 9.8 percent between April and October 1996 compared with 11.7 in the same period a year earlier.
"The forecast of 10 percent is on the high side," said Raghuraman.
CII said industrial performance was "affected by massive infrastructural bottlenecks".
